01 · The Opportunity

You are not missing anything. You are choosing to add something.

Waddell, thank you for the conversation. What you described is not a gap to patch. It is a decision to expand, and that is a different kind of project.

Henderick carries a real bench. Two general superintendents, three project managers, an architect, an interior designer, and an estimator, plus a field crew that is background checked and cleared to work in occupied schools. That team stays busy. Your point was that it is capable of more, and that you would like your people to have a fuller slate in the stretches where the public calendar runs lighter.

What makes that achievable is simple. Public work reaches you through sealed bids and cooperative contracts, so there has never been a reason to advertise. It worked. The result is that Henderick is well known to the people who write the specifications and largely unknown to everyone else. Meanwhile the private market buys the same gym floors, the same paving, the same interior upgrades, and buys them on a phone call. That audience has not met you yet. That is the entire opportunity.

The asset

A bench that can take more on

Assembled, trained, certified, and cleared. That is the hard part and it is already done. Adding volume to a team like that is a marketing question rather than a hiring one.

The material

Work that photographs itself

A finished gym floor is a mirror with a mascot in the middle of it. Very little in facilities looks like that. The material for a year of content is produced on your job sites already.

The door

Credentials that reach a different room

CCIM and CPM are commercial real estate designations. Property managers and building owners are professional peers, not cold prospects, and they own gyms, courts, lots, and amenity space with no procurement office in between.

The timing

A lane nobody is defending

Two specialist competitors are buying search results in Tennessee. On the social side the category is effectively unclaimed. Section 04 shows exactly what we found.

Gym floors go first because they are the most visible thing you do. Paving, grading, interiors, and facilities management follow the same audience through the same door.

You want the market to understand Henderick as the company that holds a standard. Recognized for expertise, not for being the low number on a sheet.

Thirty four years in the field, starting at seventeen. That is the thing no competitor can copy, and right now there is nowhere a buyer can go to find it.

Google first because the demand already exists there and is measurable. Meta once the library can support it, for the reasons laid out in section 08.

03 · The Range

Gym floors open the door. They are not the whole program.

Athletic surfaces lead because they are the most striking thing you do and because the search demand is already measurable. But the buyer who finds you for a gym floor runs an entire building, and you already handle the rest of it. Each line below is its own content stream, its own set of search terms, and its own reason for someone to call.

Lead service

Athletic Surfaces and Facilities

Indoors, gymnasium refinishing, resurfacing, replacement, game line striping, and logo painting. Outdoors, stadium fields, turf, and track surfaces, as delivered at Stratford High School.

Content angle: the transformation sequence, start to finish, on the ground and from the air. Plus the maintenance conversation almost nobody is having with facility owners.
Service line

Paving and Exterior Maintenance

Parking lot resurfacing, repaving and striping, sidewalk repair, and exterior concrete work held to public sector standards.

Content angle: the first thing every visitor sees. Curb appeal, accessibility compliance, and liability, which is language property managers respond to.
Service line

Interiors and ADA Upgrades

Painting, flooring, wall repair, cabinetry, lighting upgrades, and ADA compliant modifications, delivered without disrupting daily operations.

Content angle: accessibility work is a compliance obligation with a deadline attached, which makes it one of the most searchable services you offer.
Service line

Grading and Drainage

Grounds work, drainage correction, and durable line painting for lots, sports fields, and facility grounds.

Content angle: the work nobody sees until it fails. Standing water and failing grade are problems owners already know they have.
Service line

Facilities Management and Infrastructure

Ongoing preventive and predictive plans, routine inspection, emergency repair, and newer infrastructure work such as the EV charging build in your portfolio.

Content angle: this is the recurring revenue line. It is also the one that turns a single project client into a multi year relationship.

The gymnasium image is a Henderick project. The four service line images are visual direction showing the standard of photography this program would produce, and will be replaced with Henderick work as it is captured.

05 · The Audience

Same crew. Same standard. Six ways in.

Every buyer below needs floors refinished, fields rebuilt, courts striped, lots repaved, and interiors updated. Most of them are not bound to a public procurement calendar, and most schedule between September and May.

Segment 01 · Priority

Stadiums and athletic fields

Outdoor athletic facilities are their own line of work and you are already delivering it. Stratford High School's field is a Henderick project. Middle Tennessee has dozens of high school stadiums on aging surfaces, and at the college level TSU has publicly discussed renovating Hale Stadium, a seventy year old facility now used mainly for practice. Those projects go through procurement. Being the name already on the shortlist is what gets you invited to the table.

Segment 02

Churches with gyms

Tennessee religious construction is active, and family life centers almost always include a gym. Your Memphis competitor already lists church clients by name. These decisions happen in a committee meeting, not a bid.

Segment 03

Private and parochial schools

Tennessee has 609 private schools serving over 113,000 students, roughly two thirds religiously affiliated. Same gyms, same fields, same lots, none of the procurement process.

Segment 04

YMCAs, rec centers, clubs

Around 2,600 YMCAs and more than 5,400 Boys and Girls Club sites nationally, plus every municipal community center in Middle Tennessee.

Segment 05

Property managers and CRE

Your CCIM and CPM peers. Corporate campuses, multifamily amenity space, HOAs. Roughly three in four renters call an onsite fitness center a must have, and amenity space wears out on a schedule.

Segment 06

General contractors

Every GC building a school, church, stadium, or rec center needs a specialty sub who will not create a problem. Right now they find that sub by asking around. This makes Henderick the name they already recognize.

Segment figures from the Tennessee private school directory, YMCA of the USA, Boys and Girls Clubs of America, and the National Multifamily Housing Council. Citations in section 15.

06 · The Standard

No trends. No stunts. The work, filmed properly.

You were clear that Henderick is not going to chase a format, and we agree completely. That is not a constraint on this program. It is the premise of it.

The content that earns trust in the trades is not the content that tries hardest. It is the content that shows competence. A crew that knows exactly what it is doing, filmed by people who know exactly what they are looking at, is inherently worth watching. The audience here is facility directors, principals, business managers, and property managers. None of them are looking to be entertained. They are looking for evidence that you will not create a problem in their building.

So the standard is simple. We film your expertise, your process, and your finished work, at the same level of care your crews bring to a floor.

What we film

  • The process in order, from a worn floor to a finished room
  • Waddell and the superintendents answering the questions buyers actually ask
  • The details that prove care: a clean edge, a stencil lifting true, a joint that lines up
  • Crews working safely and cleanly inside an occupied building
  • The finished space with the lights up and the community back in it
  • Clients describing what it was like to have Henderick on site

What we will not

  • Trending sounds, dance formats, or anything built around a passing joke
  • Manufactured urgency, countdowns, or discount theater
  • Asking anyone to perform in a voice that is not their own
  • Anything that would read as unserious to a procurement officer
  • Claims the field cannot stand behind

For what it is worth, the restraint is also what works. The most watched flooring content on the internet is not stunt content. It is a camera held steady on skilled hands doing something correctly. That is a format Henderick can own without changing a thing about how the company carries itself.

08 · The Sequencing

Google first. Paid social at month three. Here is the full reasoning.

One clarification before the argument, because it matters. Everything on this page about holding until month three refers to paid social only. Your organic accounts start in month one and never pause.

From the first capture session, we are posting to Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn on a real calendar, building the Google Business Profile, and putting work in front of people. That costs no media budget and it starts immediately. What we are staging is the decision to put dollars behind Meta's auction, and only because that specific system rewards a volume of creative that does not exist yet on day one.

So the sequence is Google Ads and organic posting from month one, paid Meta added at month three. Here is why, including the part that works against us.

01

Google is where the category already transacts

Praters is running sixteen ads. Sports Floors is running nine, one of which reads Gym Floor Refinishing, Call For An Estimate. Those are Tennessee companies buying Tennessee search results for work Henderick does, today, in an auction you are not in. Someone typing that phrase has already decided to spend money. There is nothing to warm up.

02

Search converts this kind of buyer better

Across commercial and professional services, published benchmark data puts paid search conversion at 7.8 percent against 4.4 percent for paid social. In construction and engineering specifically, tracked data puts it at 5.1 percent against 1.8 percent, and separate research finds paid social visitors bounce 41 percent more often. This is a considered purchase, and search catches people at the end of the decision rather than the beginning.

03

Paid Meta rewards volume of creative, which takes time to build

Meta's own published guidance asks advertisers to keep at least twenty distinct ads running and to put twenty to thirty percent of budget into testing new ones weekly. An analysis of more than 550,000 ads found roughly five percent ever become strong performers. The paid side of Meta is a system that consumes creative. Spending there before the library exists means paying the auction to learn what a few capture sessions would show for free. Organic posting has no such constraint, which is exactly why it starts on day one.

04

The part that argues against us

We would rather say this than have you find it. Meta's published cost per lead is lower than Google's, $27.66 against $66.69 across all industries, and $41.26 against $90.92 in home improvement. If lead price were the only measure, Meta wins outright. It is not the only measure. Google leads arrive from people already shopping for the service, and in this category they convert two to four times better. The case for sequencing is intent and readiness, not cost, and we will not dress it up as something else.

05

By month three you enter the paid auction with a real library

Two months at the recommended tier puts roughly twenty finished assets in hand, which is exactly the floor Meta names, and every one of them has already run organically, so you know which ones people actually watch. You are not guessing at launch, you are promoting proven material. And because the Ad Library shows the category effectively unclaimed, Henderick enters an auction with almost no competition on the terms that matter.

09 · The Calendar

The gym floor year runs on a fixed calendar. We plan around it.

One Middle Tennessee district writes it into the request for proposals in plain language. Gym floor work happens from the last week of May through the first week of August, and scheduling for it is committed in February and March. That shape determines when we film, when we publish, and when we spend.

September to November
Athletic surface work slows. The campaign gets loud. Public gyms are in season, so that side of the calendar has room. We publish everything filmed over the summer, launch Google, and go after churches, private schools, and property managers whose schedules have nothing to do with a school year.
December and January
Winter break is a genuine production window. Two weeks with a building empty is enough for a sanding job, and your competitors already use it. We film it and we sell it. Social launches here with a full library behind it.
February to April
The booking season that sets the year. This is when districts, churches, and facility owners commit summer schedules. Every dollar of spend and every case study from the fall points at this window. Nothing else on the calendar decides as much.
May to August
Peak production for you and peak capture for us. Crews are on floors every week. This is when we bank the footage, the interviews, and the transformation sequences that carry the following twelve months.
Running underneath all of it
Your 24 hour emergency response and preventive maintenance agreements do not follow a season, and neither does the content for them. Emergency capability and predictive maintenance are their own year round story, and they are the ones that turn a project client into a standing relationship.

Year one runs slightly out of phase, and that is fine

Starting in September means the first capture sessions land after the summer gym floor season has closed. So year one begins where the work actually is: interiors, paving, grading, and the preventive and emergency jobs that carry your fall. That is not a compromise. It is the fastest way to prove the program across four service lines instead of one, and it means the search account, the audience, and a real library are already in place by February, which is the window that decides next summer.

Winter break brings the first gym floor capture in December. Summer 2027 is the first full athletic season with a camera on it, and by then none of this is starting from zero.

12 · Investment

We are recommending a retainer. Here is why, rather than assuming.

You did not ask for one, so it deserves a reason. Your own About page puts it better than we could. Your focus, in your words, is not on one off projects but on being the go to partner your clients can rely on, year after year.

Marketing works the same way and for the same reason. A single video does not open a market. What opens a market is a library that keeps working long after it is delivered, a search presence that keeps catching people at the moment they are looking, and someone accountable for both every month. A one time production package is the most expensive way to buy marketing, because everything stops the day the file is delivered.

If you would rather begin with a fixed scope production package and add the ongoing program later, we will build that instead and say so plainly. We just do not think it is the faster route to what you described.

A note on how we count. The tiers are measured in capture sessions rather than days on site. A session is one subject carried all the way through: planning it, filming it, cutting it, and publishing it. Two sessions can share a single day in the field. If we are already at a school to film a floor and Waddell is available for an interview, we shoot both and nobody drives twice. What does not compress is everything after the camera goes off, and that is the real constraint on how much finished work lands each month.

And on what each piece is. A hero piece is a complete thirty to sixty second film with a beginning and an end, the one that carries the month. A short cut is a single moment that stands on its own, a stencil lifting or a straight answer to one question. A paid variant is existing footage recut with a different opening for the ad account, which is how the Meta auction is fed without manufacturing content nobody asked for. We count these separately on purpose. A studio that promises twenty pieces a month is usually counting variants as films, and you would notice the difference before your audience did.

Why the middle tier is the recommendation

The first tier builds an audience but leaves the search results to Praters and Sports Floors for another season, and search is where the category is moving money today. The third tier is the right answer once the private market is producing and you want to scale across every service line, which is a conversation for month six or later. The middle tier does the thing that needs doing now. It builds the library and competes for search demand at the same time, then brings social into play the moment you can win there.

Those benchmarks come from the same published 2026 dataset in both directions. The Industrial and Commercial category runs $5.87 per click at an 8.2 percent conversion rate, which puts $1,500 near twenty inquiries. Home and Home Improvement runs more expensive at $8.33 per click, which puts the same budget nearer fourteen. Your work sits between the two, so fifteen to twenty five is the planning range once the account clears its first six weeks.

Two variables move the real number inside that range, and both are measurable rather than theoretical.

Auction competition sets the price

  • Cost per click is decided by how many advertisers are bidding on a term
  • The Ads Transparency Center shows a small field on these terms in Middle Tennessee
  • Fewer bidders means less upward pressure on price, which is the same reason to enter this year rather than next

Your own data replaces the estimate fast

  • No published cost per click figure exists for gym floor refinishing as a specific term. We looked.
  • Category averages are the correct starting input, and they are what the numbers above use
  • Sixty days of search term data replaces every estimate on this page with your actual number

One definition worth setting now. An inquiry is a call or a form, not a signed job. This category closes on a phone conversation and a site visit, which is the part Henderick already does well. So the figure at the top of the monthly report is not clicks and it is not inquiries. It is how many projects the private lane produced, and in which months, because that is the thing you actually asked for.

14 · Outside the Retainer

The big days get their own crew.

The retainer covers the ongoing program. Single days with their own stakes are their own production, and we keep them separate so neither gets shortchanged. A ribbon cutting at a finished gym, a school reopening, a groundbreaking, a company anniversary, a recruiting day, or a milestone with a client and their community in the room.

Event coverage

What we bring to a milestone day

Multiple cameras and a director on site, event photography across the day, a recap film delivered the same week, a social recap set for reach afterward, interview capture built into the run of show, and everything archived into the project library.

How it works

Send us the date

When one lands on the calendar, send the details and we will build it as its own proposal against the actual scope. No price is attached here because the right number depends entirely on the room, the schedule, and what you need afterward.

16 · The Details

Clean and simple.

01

Access and scheduling

We work off your production schedule. Give us the sites and the dates and we build the shoot calendar around jobs already happening, so filming never adds a day to a project or slows a crew down.

02

Site safety and permission

Our crew follows your site protocols and carries its own insurance. Work on school or government property is filmed only with written client permission in hand, which we help you request.

03

Approvals

Nothing is published without your review. Two revision rounds on each deliverable, with additional rounds billed at standard hourly rate.

04

Ownership

You own the final delivered work. Walton Creative Group retains master files for twelve months and may use the work in portfolio and marketing with your approval.

05

Ad accounts

Google Ads and Meta accounts are created under Henderick ownership from day one. We manage them. You keep them, along with every dollar of learning inside them, whatever happens later.

17 · Next Steps

February decides next summer. Everything that needs to be ready by then starts now.

Districts, churches, and facility owners commit their summer schedules in February and March. A search account that has been running since the fall, an audience that has watched your crews work, and a library of finished projects are not things that can be assembled in January.
